newsitem.title: CANADA: Bre-X fallout flattens Canadian mining shares.
newsitem.headline: Bre-X fallout flattens Canadian mining shares.

text.p: The carnage continued in Canadian stock markets on Thursday as shaken investors dumped precious metals stocks after the news that Bre-X Minerals Ltd.'s glittering Indonesian gold discovery might not be the motherlode after all.
Bre-X stock, which was halted all day Wednesday, resumed trading late Thursday and dove C$12 to re-open at C$3.50, wiping about C$3 billion ($2.2 billion) from its market value.
Calgary, Alberta-based Bre-X said on Wednesday the resources from the Busang gold deposit in Indonesia, billed as the largest gold find this century, may have been overstated.
"Most of the street is just ready to hang themselves. You got a lot of retail in this thing, big funds -- Fidelity, Appaloosa," noted one U.S. arbitrager.
On Thursday, the Toronto Stock Exchange's precious metals index posted its biggest one-day drop since Sept. 7, 1993, plummeting 906.93 points, or 8.66 percent, to 9,559.92.

Mining stocks dragged down the whole market, with the broad-based TSE 300 Composite Index tumbling 191.21, or 3.12 percent, to close at 5,931.63. It was the largest one-day drop since October 20, 1987, the day after so-called Black Monday when the TSE 300 lost 220.90 points.

"You are going to get margin calls. You are going to get people unwinding positions (in small miners). You are going to get mutual funds selling because they have no choice," said Deacon Capital Corp. trader Sonny Lennon.

Traders said mutual funds were probably seeing a deluge of redemptions by edgy investors in their resource and speculative funds. Mutual fund company AGF Management B class shares dropped C$2 to C$36.50.

Several large funds wrote down their investment in Bre-X to C$1 or C$2 a share, while some wrote off all their holdings. CIBC Precious Metals fund wrote its holding, comprising 8 percent of the fund, down to zero.

The Bre-X saga, with its promise of instant wealth, captured the Canadian imagination like few others. The stock soared from mere pennies to C$250 before splitting 10-for-1, prompting investors to buy other small mining firms in droves in the hope of finding another Bre-X.

The stunning reversal in Bre-X's fortunes may have crushed the credibility of the small mining group for a long time to come. At this stage, traders and investors are uncertain who or what to believe.
"The psychology's been totally dented," one dealer said.

Yamana Resources, which has a property near Busang, said uncertainties in Papua New Guinea, Indonesia and in gold equity markets prevented it from getting funding for its acquisition of Australia's Union Mining NL.

One arbitrager said the experience would probably breed a new scepticism in the investing public, with calls for more checks and sounder information. "It's going to make it a lot harder for companies to hype up their stocks," he said.
The bloodbath was even worse on the Vancouver and Alberta stock markets, both of which are weighted toward mining.
The Alberta exchange's Combined Value index was down 88.06 points at 2,711.79. On Wednesday, the index fell 89.79 points to 2,799.85, its largest one-day drop since October 1987.
The Vancouver exchange's Composite index dropped 56.24 points to 1,130.46 after falling 79 points to 1,186.7 on Wednesday, its biggest tumble since the 1987 market crash.
A number of miners with Indonesian properties suffered from the sell-off. But many exploring far from the jungles of Borneo were pounded as well.
Mexican gold player Farralon Resources dropped C$1.40 to C$9, while base metals miner Fenway Resources Ltd., which is exploring in the Philippines, shed C$1 to C$8.35 on the Vancouver exchange.
